extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, PTO/OED disciplinary counsel, and administrative adjudicators handling practitioner discipline
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing disciplinary proceedings against patent practitioners before the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (OED), including service, default, definitions of misconduct, and factors for imposing sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of Complaint (37 C.F.R. § 11.35)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may serve a complaint on a respondent '[b]y mailing a copy of the complaint by 'Express Mail,' first-class mail, or any delivery service that provides ability to confirm delivery or attempted delivery to .. [a] respondent who is a registered practitioner at the address provided to OED pursuant to § 11.11,' or if the respondent is not registered, to the respondent's last address known to the Director. If the complaint cannot be delivered in accordance with paragraph (a), the Director shall serve the respondent by causing an appropriate notice to be published in the Official Gazette for two consecutive weeks, in which case, the time for filing an answer shall be thirty days from the second publication of the notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use registered address of record per §11.11; if mail is returned/unclaimed, effect service by two consecutive publications in the Official Gazette and set answer deadline 30 days from the second publication. Examples in the record: complaint sent by certified mail to address of record, returned as 'unclaimed' and service completed by publication (May 29 and June 5, 2012).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to keep contact information current (37 C.F.R. § 11.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: An attorney or agent registered to appear before the PTO must notify the 'Director of his or her postal address for his or her office, ... e-mail addresses ... , and business telephone number, as well as every change to any of said addresses or telephone numbers within thirty days of the date of the change.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to update address can result in mail being returned and service via publication; service by mail to the address 'reasonably believed' to be the practitioner's may be sufficient if practitioner failed to update per §11.11.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default for failure to answer (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent's failure to file a timely answer constitutes an admission of the allegations in the Complaint, and a default judgment may be entered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If served properly and respondent does not answer, the hearing officer may enter default; default operates as admission of each allegation. In motions for default when respondent has not appeared, it may be unnecessary to allow additional time to respond (see Bovard v. Uland).

rubrics_metrics.name: Service when certified mail returned (publication alternative)
rubrics_metrics.description: If complaint mailed to address of record is returned (e.g., 'unclaimed'/'unable to forward'), the Director may serve by publishing a notice in two consecutive issues of the PTO Official Gazette and proceed with the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication triggers a 30-day answer period from the second publication; certificate of service and any alternative mailing attempts should be documented in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.23(b)(4) — dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes engaging in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting purported payments (checks or electronic fund transfers) to the PTO that are subsequently returned for insufficient funds qualifies as conduct involving dishonesty/fraud/misrepresentation where the practitioner knew or should have known funds were insufficient (as found in this case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.23(b)(5) — conduct prejudicial to administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes engaging in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to make good on returned checks/EFTs submitted in connection with client patent applications, and thereby depriving the PTO of funds necessary to perform its duties, can be prejudicial to the administration of justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.23(a) — disreputable or gross misconduct
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting payments to the PTO when the practitioner had insufficient funds — conduct that may also violate state criminal statutes (e.g., Va. Code § 18.2-181) — can constitute disreputable or gross misconduct under Rule 10.23(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 10.77(c) — neglect of a legal matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Proscribes neglect of a legal matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing clients' patent applications to become abandoned due to failure to pay the necessary patent fees is neglect of a legal matter under Rule 10.77(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of state criminal check statutes as evidence of intent (Va. Code §§ 18.2-181, 18.2-183)
rubrics_metrics.description: Virginia statutes state that knowingly drawing a check without sufficient funds can be larceny (Va. Code § 18.2-181), and that a returned check is prima facie evidence of intent to defraud or knowledge of insufficient funds unless paid within five days after written notice (Va. Code § 18.2-183).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These state-law provisions may be used as evidence to support findings of intent or knowledge when assessing practitioner misconduct involving returned checks or dishonored electronic transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for determining sanction (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining the appropriate sanction or penalty, the Tribunal must consider: (1) whether the practitioner has violated a duty owed to a client, the public, the legal system, or the profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct; and (4) the existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these four factors to the totality of the conduct. In this case the Director argued duties were breached, the acts were intentional/knowing, actual injuries were significant (over $5,000 owed), and aggravating factors existed; only absence of prior discipline was a mitigating factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors (ABA Standards §§ 9.22, 9.32 referenced)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include: a pattern of misconduct, multiple offenses, refusal to acknowledge wrongful nature of conduct, substantial experience in the practice of law, and indifference to making restitution (Standard § 9.22). Mitigating factors include absence of prior disciplinary record (Standard § 9.32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify applicable aggravators/mitigators and weigh them under §11.54(b). The Director relied on these aggravating factors to support a multi-year suspension; only lack of prior record was mitigating in this matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of attorney disciplinary proceedings is to protect the public and the justice system from lawyers who are derelict in their professional duties (citing ABA Standard § 1.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions should be tailored to protect the public and maintain the integrity of the profession; prior case law and comparative sanctions can inform appropriate discipline (court cites analogous cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on disciplinary remedies (statutory authority, 35 U.S.C. § 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: This Tribunal has limited authority under statute and 'has previously been held that this Tribunal has no authority to enter an order other than for exclusion or suspension of restitution by virtue of the limitations set forth in 35 U.S.C. § 32.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies should be chosen within the statutory limits (suspension/exclusion and related relief that the Tribunal is authorized to award); counsel should not seek sanctions beyond the Tribunal's statutory authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and notice of disciplinary action
rubrics_metrics.description: The facts and circumstances of the proceeding shall be fully published in the Patent and Trademark Office's official publication (Official Gazette).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disciplinary outcomes are publicized; publication may be part of the sanction's effect on reputation and the public record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-discipline responsibilities and reinstatement (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.60)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplined practitioners have responsibilities set out in § 11.58 and may petition for reinstatement under § 11.60.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanction orders should direct attention to these regulatory obligations; respondents may appeal per § 11.55 and may seek reinstatement in accordance with §11.60 after suspension/exclusion periods.
